title: Slavery by Another Name: The Re-Enslavement of Black Americans from the Civil War to World War II
author: Douglas A. Blackmon
target_audience: Students and scholars of African-American studies
General audiences seeking to understand the legacy of slavery and racial injustice
Those interested in social justice and civil rights
core_themes: Systematic re-enslavement of African-Americans after the Civil War
Exploitation through convict leasing and peonage systems
Racism and white supremacy in post-emancipation America
The complicity of government, legal systems, and corporations
The enduring legacy of forced labor on Black families and communities
primary_purpose: To expose and document the little-known history of how slavery, in various forms, persisted in the United States long after the Emancipation Proclamation, through mechanisms such as convict leasing, peonage, and forced labor—revealing how millions of Black Americans were re-enslaved and how these systems shaped the modern American South.

structure_format.narrative_style: Investigative, historical, and narrative-driven; based on scholarship and personal stories
structure_format.organization: Chronological with thematic focus, combining large-scale analysis with detailed individual case studies
features: Contextualization within American legal and social systems

key_concepts_lessons: Slavery in America did not end with the Civil War, but evolved into new systems of forced labor.
The convict leasing system systematically criminalized Black life and funneled African-Americans into forced labor.
Local and federal governments, as well as corporations, maintained and profited from these unjust systems.
False criminal charges and debt peonage were common tools for re-enslavement.
This history has been largely omitted from popular narratives about American freedom and progress.
The legacy of this era continues to affect American society, law, and race relations.
notable_features: Combines archival research with compelling storytelling
Shines light on a suppressed chapter of American history
Inspiration for a PBS documentary of the same name
cultural_historical_context: Published in the late 2000s, the book challenged the dominant narrative of post-Civil War America by revealing vast systems of forced labor that mirrored slavery. It arrived amid national conversations on race, criminal justice, and the historical roots of mass incarceration.
reception_impact: Winner of the 2009 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction
Widely praised for groundbreaking research and narrative power
Influenced scholarly and public understanding of American history
Inspired ongoing discussions about the legacy of forced labor and mass incarceration
Some critics argue that it could overstate the scale or diminish the achievements of emancipation, but it is largely celebrated for bringing crucial truths to light
